title: A blackened cooking vessel
body: Riya helps her family cook on an LPG stove. Over a few weeks she notices that the flame, which used to be blue, has become yellow and that the bottoms of the cooking vessels have turned black with a powdery deposit. Her teacher explains that a gas stove has inlets for air so that the fuel mixes with enough oxygen before it burns. When fuel burns in a sufficient supply of oxygen, it gives a clean blue flame and the carbon in it is converted to carbon dioxide. When the supply of air is limited, even saturated hydrocarbons undergo incomplete combustion and give a sooty flame. Riya's teacher also mentions that fuels such as coal and petroleum contain some nitrogen and sulphur, and burning them forms oxides of sulphur and nitrogen, which are major pollutants.

title: Oil, water and soap
body: Aman takes about 10 mL of water in each of two test tubes, A and B, and adds a drop of cooking oil to each. To test tube B he adds a few drops of soap solution. He shakes both tubes vigorously for the same time and then leaves them undisturbed. In tube A the oil soon separates as a layer on top of the water, while in tube B the oil stays spread through the water for much longer. His teacher explains that a soap molecule has two ends with different properties: an ionic end that interacts with water (hydrophilic) and a long hydrocarbon tail that interacts with oil (hydrophobic). Inside water, soap molecules form clusters called micelles, which trap the oily dirt so that it can be rinsed away.
